hints: XOR-ing everything no longer gives one answer; it gives a ^ b mixed together. Since a ≠ b, that result has at least one 1-bit. What does a 1-bit there tell you about a and b?

XOR then split: let x = a ^ b. Take its lowest set bit low = x & -x; a and b differ on that bit. Split all numbers into two groups by that bit and XOR each group separately; pairs stay together and cancel, leaving a in one group and b in the other.

1. x = XOR of all numbers (equals a ^ b).
  2. low = x & (−x), the lowest set bit.
  3. a = XOR of all v with (v & low) != 0.
  4. b = x ^ a.
  5. Return [min(a,b), max(a,b)].

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Count occurrences with a HashMap, collect the two values with count 1, and sort them.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: XOR all to get a ^ b, split by one differing bit, XOR each half.

explain: Sample [3,8,3,5]: XOR of all is 8 ^ 5 = 1101 (13). Its lowest set bit is 1. Numbers with bit 0 set: 3, 3, 5 → XOR gives 5. The other one is 13 ^ 5 = 8. Sorted: [5,8]. Pairs always land in the same group because equal numbers have equal bits, so they cancel inside their group. Edge case: when x has only bit 31 set (e.g. −231 and 0), x & -x still works in Java because −x wraps to x; just don't use Math.abs here.
recognize: 'Exactly two values appear once, the rest twice, O(1) space' → XOR all, then split by a set bit of the XOR.
